query: For a multi-phase eutectic high-entropy alloy exposed to simultaneous wear and corrosion at elevated temperature, what single mechanistic hypothesis could explain the accelerated coupled degradation and why it occurs? Specify a controlled comparison capable of distinguishing the proposed explanation, predict the changes in total degradation and the individual wear and corrosion responses relative to a matched baseline, define the relevant boundary conditions, identify supporting evidence, and give a clear falsification criterion.

generation.hypothesis: In the multiphase eutectic high‐entropy alloy, the heterogeneous microstructure creates phase boundaries with significantly different electrochemical potentials. Under elevated temperature conditions, the protective oxide films that normally form on these distinct phases are cyclically broken down by mechanical wear. This continuous removal exposes fresh, galvanically active interfaces, which rapidly accelerate both localized corrosion and abrasive wear when acting in tandem.
generation.material_initial_state: As-cast multiphase eutectic HEA exhibiting alternating soft (e.g., FCC) and hard (e.g., BCC/B2) lamellae with initially protective, but fragile, oxide films forming in elevated temperature environments.
generation.intervention: Expose the alloy to simultaneous frictional wear and a corrosive environment (e.g., chloride-containing acidic solution) at elevated temperature (e.g., 700–800 °C) versus controlled baseline conditions.
generation.conditions: High temperature (700–800 °C) under a controlled corrosive electrolyte (e.g., chloride-containing sulfuric acid) combined with constant mechanical sliding (wear) that cyclically removes surface oxides. Baseline comparisons include testing under isolated wear or isolated corrosion conditions or testing a chemically homogeneous single‐phase HEA under the same combined conditions.
generation.structural_mediator: The phase boundaries inherent to the eutectic microstructure that result in local microgalvanic cells, where differences in corrosion potential between neighboring phases destabilize the protective oxide layers.
generation.mechanism: Elevated temperature accelerates oxide formation; however, mechanical wear preferentially erodes these transient films. Due to inherent microgalvanic differences at phase boundaries, the damaged sites are quickly re-exposed to aggressive corrosion, resulting in a feedback loop where corrosion further degrades mechanical integrity, and vice versa, leading to accelerated overall degradation.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the baseline (either isolated wear, isolated corrosion, or a homogeneous single‐phase alloy under identical conditions), the alloy will show a super-additive increase in total material loss, deeper and more localized wear tracks, and increased corrosion current densities. Specifically, the coupling of wear and corrosion will yield higher mass loss and more severe surface degradation than would be predicted by simply adding the individual effects.
generation.baseline: A comparable alloy system tested under: (i) isolated wear (inert atmospheric conditions) at the same temperature, (ii) isolated corrosion (without mechanical wear), or (iii) a single-phase, chemically homogeneous HEA under combined conditions.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis holds for eutectic high-entropy alloy systems with distinct phase boundaries and protective oxide formation at elevated temperature (700–800 °C) when exposed simultaneously to mechanical wear and a corrosive electrolyte. Deviations in microstructural homogeneity or testing below the critical temperature may not exhibit the same coupling effect.
generation.uncertainty: The exact magnitude of the accelerated degradation is uncertain and may depend on the specific nature of the phase boundary potentials, the kinetics of oxide formation, and the aggressiveness of the corrosive medium. Quantitative differences between alloys with slightly varying phase fractions or compositions remain to be determined.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples of the same eutectic HEA: one with the multiphase microstructure and one processed to achieve a more homogeneous single-phase microstructure (if possible by thermal processing or alloy design). Subject both sets to identical testing conditions: (a) simultaneous wear and corrosion at 700–800 °C in a chloride-containing acidic solution, (b) identical isolated wear tests in inert conditions, and (c) isolated corrosion tests without wear. Compare the total degradation (measured by mass loss, depth of wear tracks, and surface morphology) and electrochemical corrosion parameters.
measurements: Wear track depth and morphology (via SEM)
Electrochemical impedance spectroscopy for passive film stability
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the multiphase eutectic HEA does not display a super-additive (greater than the sum of isolated wear and corrosion effects) degradation under combined conditions compared to either baseline condition or to a more homogeneous single-phase alloy, then the mechanistic hypothesis attributing accelerated coupled degradation to oxide film breakdown at phase boundaries is falsified.

A Promising New Class of High-Temperature Alloys: Eutectic High-Entropy Alloys

Abstract: High-entropy alloys (HEAs) can have either high strength or high ductility, and a simultaneous achievement of both still constitutes a tough challenge. The inferior castability and compositional segregation of HEAs are also obstacles for their technological applications. To tackle these problems, here we proposed a novel strategy to design HEAs using the eutectic alloy concept, i.e. to achieve a microstructure composed of alternating soft fcc and hard bcc phases. As a manifestation of this concept, an AlCoCrFeNi2.1 (atomic portion) eutectic high-entropy alloy (EHEA) was designed. The as-cast EHEA possessed a fine lamellar fcc/B2 microstructure, and showed an unprecedented combination of high tensile ductility and high fracture strength at room temperature. The excellent mechanical properties could be kept up to 700°C. This new alloy design strategy can be readily adapted to large-scale industrial production of HEAs with simultaneous high fracture strength and high ductility.

High-Temperature Wear Behaviour of Spark Plasma Sintered AlCoCrFeNiTi0.5 High-Entropy Alloy

Abstract: AbstractIn this study, the wear behaviour of a powder metallurgically produced AlCoCrFeNiTi0.5 high-entropy alloy (HEAs) is investigated at elevated temperatures. Spark plasma sintering (SPS) of inert gas atomised feedstock enables the production of dense bulk material. The microstructure evolution and phase formation are analysed. The high cooling rate in the atomisation process results in spherical powder with a microstructure comprising two finely distributed body-centred cubic phases. An additional phase with a complex crystal structure precipitates during SPS processing, while no coarsening of microstructural features occurs. The wear resistance under reciprocating wear conditions increases at elevated temperatures due to the formation of a protective oxide layer under atmospherical conditions. Additionally, the coefficient of friction (COF) slightly decreases with increasing temperature. SPS processing is suitable for the production of HEA bulk material.
